t: Design an Expression Tree With Evaluate Function: Stack Building and Modular Nodes
o: Postfix notation lists operands before their operators, so ["4","5","7","2","+","-","*"] encodes 4 * (5 - (7 + 2)). Reading left to right, an operator always applies to the two MOST RECENTLY completed expressions — exactly what a stack tracks: push a leaf node for every number, and for an operator pop the right child first, then the left, attach both, and push the combined subtree. The single remaining stack entry is the root, and calling evaluate() on it recursively computes -16 for the example. Constraints are tiny (fewer than 100 tokens, intermediate values within 10^9), so performance is irrelevant; the real challenges are getting the construction mechanics right and honoring the follow-up request for a modular design where new operators need no changes to existing code.
k: Postfix removes all precedence ambiguity: building the tree needs no parsing tricks, just pop-two-push-one whenever an operator appears.
The first pop is the RIGHT child and the second is the LEFT child — swapping them silently breaks subtraction and division.
Integer division must truncate toward zero (e.g. -16 / 7 = -2); languages disagree here, so be explicit.
The modularity follow-up is answered by polymorphism: one evaluate() per operator class keeps the builder untouched when operators are added.

a.n: Approach 1: Stack Build with a Single Dispatching Node Class
a.i: Represent every node uniformly: its value holds either an integer (leaf) or an operator character (internal). evaluate() checks which kind it stores and either returns the number or recurses on both children and applies the operator via a switch. This keeps the whole solution compact and is perfectly adequate at this input size.
s: Scan tokens left to right; push a leaf holding the parsed integer for each number.
On an operator token, pop the right child, then the left child, wrap them in an internal node and push it.
Return the last stack entry as the root; evaluate() returns leaf values and recursively combines children, dividing with truncation toward zero.
a.t: O(L) — each of the L tokens is pushed and popped once and evaluation visits every node once (L < 100).
a.sp: O(L) — build-stack entries plus recursion depth bounded by the tree height.

a.i: Give addition, subtraction, multiplication and division their own subclasses of Node, each implementing evaluate(). Adding exponentiation later means writing one new class and registering it in the builder factory — no existing class changes, exactly the extensibility the follow-up requests. Construction is otherwise identical to Approach 1.
s: Define a base Node with an abstract evaluate().
Implement NumNode plus one class per operator combining left.evaluate() with right.evaluate().
In buildTree, look up each token in a symbol-to-class factory: numbers create NumNode, operators pop two children and instantiate the matching class.
a.t: O(L) — same single pass over tokens and one visit per node during evaluation.
a.sp: O(L) — stack during construction, recursion during evaluation, one object per token.

w: Lead with the stack mechanics since that is the heart of the problem, then volunteer the polymorphic design if asked about extensibility. Frequent mistakes: attaching popped children in the wrong order (breaking - and /), using floor division where truncation toward zero is required for negative intermediates, and returning a number from buildTree instead of a Node exposing evaluate(). Natural follow-ups: convert an infix expression by running shunting-yard first, support unary minus, or make evaluate() accept a variable-binding map.
